column1: # The exercise catalogue every workout is built from.
# Sessions are assembled from these rows by WorkoutPlanner, not written by the
# model. A generated plan can hallucinate an exercise, prescribe 40 reps of
# something nobody should do 40 reps of, or return nothing at all on a bad day;
# a table cannot. The model's job in this feature is the coaching sentence, and
# Format, pipe-delimited, one exercise per line:

column9: cue

column1: # key         Stable identifier. Referenced by workout_session_exercise, so
#             renaming one silently rewrites what old sessions say the user did.
#             The load-bearing column. It is what lets the planner fill a
#             balanced session, and what makes the Replace sheet's promise --
#             "each of these keeps the same job in your session" -- literally
#             true rather than marketing. Alternatives are drawn from the same
#             pattern at the same or lower equipment tier.
#             What you must HAVE to do this. A user's answer is a set; a row is
#             offered only if its single requirement is in that set. "none" is
#             therefore always available, which is what keeps a kit-less
#             beginner from getting a short session full of empty slots.
#             The MINIMUM level. An intermediate user can be given beginner
#             rows; a beginner is never given intermediate ones.
#             A plank prescribed as "30 reps" is wrong in a way no amount of
# base_reps   The beginner-baseline dose. WorkoutPlanner scales it by level and
#             by how the last sessions were rated, so this is a starting point
# cue         One sentence, shown only once the exercise is in front of you.
#             The single thing most likely to keep the movement safe.
# INVARIANT, enforced by WorkoutCatalogTest: every pattern has at least one
# equipment=none, level=beginner row. Break it and a beginner with no equipment
# gets a session that is quietly short rather than one that fails loudly.

column9: Sit back like there is a chair behind you and keep your knees tracking over your toes.
Touch the seat lightly and stand back up. Do not drop onto it.
Most of your weight on the front foot. The back leg is a kickstand.
Step back rather than forward so the front knee stays calm.
Hold the weight against your chest and let it counterbalance you.
Lower straight down. Your back knee should nearly touch the floor.
Push your knees out against the band the whole way down and up.
Stop just short of locking your knees at the top.
Brace as if bracing for a punch before every single rep.
Rear foot elevated. Keep the front shin close to vertical.
Squeeze at the top for a full second before lowering.
Push your hips back, not down. Your shins stay near vertical.
Keep your hips level. Do not let the free side drop.
Lower as slowly as you can control, then push back with your hands.
Weights stay close to your legs. Stop when your hamstrings say so.
Tuck your chin and finish with your ribs down, not flared.
The band pulls your hips back. You pull them forward.
Take the slack out of the bar before you pull. No jerking off the floor.
Stop at a straight line. There is nothing to gain past it.
Body in one line from knees to head. Elbows at roughly 45 degrees.
Hands on a table or wall. The higher the hands the easier it gets.
Elbows at 45 degrees and your body in one straight line throughout.
Hips high, crown of the head towards the floor between your hands.
The floor caps the range, which is kind to a cranky shoulder.
Press slightly forward of your ears, not behind your head.
Anchor behind you and press to full arm length without locking hard.
Use a spotter or safety pins. Touch the chest, do not bounce.
A slight bend in the elbows the whole way. This is not a press.
Face down, drag your elbows back along the floor and squeeze your shoulder blades.
Lift your chest and thighs a few centimetres only. Look at the floor.
Hold a solid frame, lean back, and pull your chest to your hands.
Under a sturdy table. Body straight, pull the chest to the edge.
Pull to your ribs, not your shoulder. Shoulders down and back.
Light weight. Lead with the elbows and stop level with your back.
Pull to the ribs and pause for a beat before letting it back out.
Straight arms. Pull the band to your chest and open across.
Pull the bar to your collarbone and let your shoulder blades travel.
Start from a dead hang and pull your chest towards the bar.
Press your lower back into the floor and keep it there the whole set.
Ribs down, hips level, and keep breathing.
Move slowly. Your hips should not rock at all.
Stack your shoulders and hips and push the floor away.
Lower back glued down. If it lifts, raise your legs higher.
One weight, walk tall, and refuse to lean towards it.
Stand side on to the anchor and resist the twist as you press out.
Turn from the ribs. Your arms are just holding on.
Drive the knees to hip height and keep the arms moving.
Wide steps side to side. Land softly through the whole foot.
Land quietly with soft knees. Quiet feet means good landings.
Fast feet, tall chest. Stop the set when your form goes not when it hurts.
Step back instead of jumping back if your lower back starts to sag.
Steady effort you could hold a short conversation through.
Legs, then back, then arms. Reverse that order coming forward.
Move one vertebra at a time and let your breath set the pace.
Tuck your tailbone first. The stretch should move to the front of the hip.
Long lunge, drop the elbow inside the front foot, then open to the ceiling.
Turn from the mid back and let your eyes follow your hand.
Drive the knee past the toes with the heel stubbornly down.
Go wider than feels necessary. Narrow grips are how shoulders get pinched.
